title: Early retirees on a marketplace plan lose the ACA premium credit in 70-88% of pre-Medicare years (cross-area: decumulation/sim, not the tax formula)
location: crates/firesight-core/src/decumulation.rs:73 (ACA_PLANNING_MARGIN = 0.02) and :1192-1200 (fills MAGI to 98% of the cliff; drops protection once forced income is over it); crates/firesight-core/src/sim/year.rs:582-594 (January estimate of investment income = last year's), :458 (January rebalance gains), :803-807 (advance credit)
evidence:
The credit and cliff arithmetic in tax::compute is correct (see verified list). The system outcome is not. Repro: /tmp/fs-audit-tax/ret_tx.json = examples/dual-income-family.json changed to a retired couple born 1966 (already_retired, TX, no jobs/children/events, cash 14k, taxable 900k with basis 500k, traditional 700k + 500k, Roth 150k), all other settings as in the example (tax_aware, fill_to_bracket 0.12, mind_aca true). `firesight trace <file> --path N --json` for N = 0..29, tallying tax_returns for the full ACA years 2027-2030 (120 household-years per variant):
- example settings (mirror location, annual rebalance, glide): 105/120 years (88%) with zero credit; mean credit $3,896 against about $29-32k available; 27 of the misses land at 400-440% FPL.
- tax_efficient + rebalance never + no glide: 83/120 (69%) zero credit, 59 of them at 400-440% FPL.
- withdrawal_order conventional (no ACA logic at all): 68/120 (57%) zero credit, mean credit $15,913.
Examples: path 0, 2027: MAGI 86,956 = 403.15% of FPL 21,569, credit 0 (traditional withdrawals 68,923 + investment income 16,335 against a January estimate near 13.9k; the 2% cushion is about $1,700). Path 1, 2028: MAGI 88,737 = 406.38%, credit 0. Path 0, 2028: January rebalance gains 143,479 put forced MAGI over the cliff, protection is dropped ('nothing to protect') and the 12% bracket is filled with 139,206 of traditional withdrawals, MAGI 305,875. The advance credit is then repaid in full the next April (correct under 2026 law), which raises the next year's withdrawals.
Headline effect (`firesight run --paths 2000`, same seed): default tax_aware: success 88.2%, median lifetime tax $375,987. Conventional: success 89.4%, lifetime tax $276,373. The 'tax-aware' default is worse than the naive order on both. Between 300% and 400% FPL each extra dollar of MAGI already costs 12% tax + 9.96% credit = 22%, so filling up to the cliff edge has no payoff even when it works.
For a couple retiring at 60 this overstates health costs by roughly $25k a year for 4-5 years; for a retire-at-50 household it is 15 years.
fix: In plan_year: (1) when on the marketplace, do not fill the ordinary bracket with traditional withdrawals or conversions beyond what spending needs; score candidates with effective_marginal_rate (tax plus credit lost) rather than the bracket rate. (2) Use a cushion sized to the estimate error (for example 10% of the cliff, or 2 standard deviations of investment income) and fund the remainder from cash, taxable basis and Roth. (3) Add a fourth-quarter true-up: recompute MAGI from year-to-date actuals and switch remaining withdrawals to Roth/cash if the cliff is within reach. (4) In ACA years skip or cap the January rebalance in the taxable bucket when its gains would cross the cliff (rebalance inside traditional/Roth first), and keep cliff protection on when the only thing over the cliff is a discretionary action. Add a regression test: retired couple at 60 with ample taxable basis receives a credit in at least 90% of pre-65 years.

title: Dynamic spending rules are anchored on the first retirement year's (bridge) withdrawal rate, so they cut on-plan households early, overspend late, and lower success below constant-real (explains the 128% / 154% anomaly)
location: crates/firesight-core/src/decumulation.rs:351-353 (initial_withdrawal_rate set from year-1 planned withdrawal), :360-382 (Guardrails), :383-403 (VanguardDynamic default rate = iwr), :409-427 (FloorCeiling); inputs built in crates/firesight-core/src/sim/year.rs:631-657
evidence: NOT an accounting bug: spend_planned = baseline discretionary + non-discretionary actually incurred (month.rs:379-383), so delivered/planned > 1 only when the rule's multiple > 1. The cause is the anchor. iwr = (budget - other income)/portfolio in the first retired year, where budget includes temporary costs (mortgage P&I, children/college, pre-65 health at full price) and other income excludes Social Security not yet claimed. The funded test that allowed retirement treats those as lumps and counts PV of SS, so iwr is a bridge rate, not a sustainable one: dual-income path 3 iwr = 6.98% (budget 155,730 / portfolio 2,231,803); already-retired 62/60 couple iwr = 6.43%. Consequences, all reproduced: (1) Early cuts on plan-expected drawdown: college raises budget 156.8k -> 182.7k and the portfolio is drawn down as planned, rate 9.6% > 1.2*iwr, cut -11.7% in 2045; discretionary is then 0 for 2046-2055. Per retirement year (1000 paths, dual example): share of paths below 90% of plan is 30% in year 3, 45% in years 6-9. (2) Cuts persist for decades after SS starts because the raise is 10% of the residual withdrawal: path 3, 2058: SS 86,890 vs budget 107,975, w = 7.7k on a 1.37M portfolio (0.56%), raise = +0.7% of spending; multiple stays 0.87-0.95 from age 68 to 83 while the portfolio grows 1.4M -> 2.7M. (3) Late-life overspending: raises continue until withdrawals reach 0.8*iwr = 5.6% of the portfolio on top of SS, and cuts are disabled in the last 15 years; median delivered/planned by retirement year: 0.95 (yr 6-9), 1.18 (yr 18), 1.45 (yr 30+). Landlord example (VanguardDynamic, rate=None -> iwr 4.19% of portfolio + all other income, +5%/yr): path 0 multiple reaches 4.88x budget (174k vs 36k) at year 43; median ratio 2.1-2.3 after year 36. (4) Success is WORSE than constant-real, which a flexible rule should never be: `firesight run examples/dual-income-family.json` = 83.2% success, 127.6% delivered, 70.1% of paths with a year < 90%; same file with spending_rule {type: constant_real} = 87.8%, 98.1%, 12.2%. vanguard_dynamic(rate null) = 69.7%; vanguard_dynamic(rate 0.035) = 92.6% (proves the default anchor is the problem). Already-retired couple 62/60 with $1.54M (/tmp/fs-audit-ledger/p_s5_retired.json): guardrails 88.0% success, 143.4% delivered, p10 terminal NW $0; constant_real 96.9%, p10 $678k. With partner_offset_years=4 the iwr is set while the partner still earns (3.75%), so the partner's planned retirement trips the guardrail: 88.0% of retired paths have a year < 90% vs 5.4% under constant_real. Failed guardrails paths had a HIGHER median early-retirement real return (5.2%) than successful ones (4.6%).
fix: Stop anchoring on current-withdrawal / portfolio. Use the funded test's own quantities, which are already recomputed each January (State::requirement): funded ratio FR_t = wealth_t / requirement_t (requirement nets lumps for mortgage and children and the PV of income not yet started). Guardrails: cut the discretionary multiple by `adjust` when FR_t < FR_0*(1-upper), raise when FR_t > FR_0*(1+lower), where adjust applies to total spending rather than to the residual withdrawal. VanguardDynamic / FloorCeiling with rate=None: default to the trigger's withdrawal_rate applied to (portfolio + PV future income - lumps) instead of the year-1 rate; never add already-counted income on top. Feed the rule a budget net of the ACA credit (next finding). Add a regression test that guardrails success >= constant_real success on the example profiles. Reporting: keep planned = baseline budget at multiple 1, but report two numbers instead of one ratio of sums: shortfall ratio = sum(min(delivered, planned))/sum(planned) (measured: dual 94.2%, landlord 97.2%, early-career 96.9%) and extra spending above plan as a separate share; the headline must never exceed 100%.

title: Home equity is never tapped: homeowners are scored as 'depleted' while holding a house worth ~$0.9M, so owning cuts the success rate by ~9 points versus renting
location: crates/firesight-core/src/sim/month.rs:1175-1205 (settle: when nothing is left to sell, essentials are cut to zero and housing costs pile up as an overdraft; the home is never sold); crates/firesight-core/src/sim/trigger.rs:94-101 (wealth); no downsizing/last-resort sale exists anywhere in sim/
evidence: Paired buy-vs-rent on examples/dual-income-family.json (5,000 paired paths): `firesight compare dual-own.json rent.patch.json` where the patch removes the buy_home event. Owning: success 82.9%, depletion 17.1%, median FI age 51.83, p10 terminal net worth $905,717. Renting: success 92.3%, depletion 7.7%, FI 50.08, p10 terminal NW $195,814. So the owner is richer at p10 by $710k and at the median by $117k, yet 'fails' 9.4 points more often. Scratch tool /tmp/fs-audit-work-home/scratch/src/bin/pair.rs (2,000 traced paths): in the owner run 16.8% of paths deplete, and 16.7% of ALL paths are depleted while holding >$100k of home equity; home equity at the month investable hits zero is p10 $479k / p50 $926k / p90 $1.83M in today's dollars. Adding a sell_property event at age 80 with then_rent 2,400 (sell80.patch.json) lifts success 82.9% -> 90.7% (rescued 400, harmed 7), i.e. 7.9 of the 9.4 points are purely the locked equity. Same sign on early-career-saver (86.5% own vs 88.3% rent; p10 terminal NW $785k vs $0). A single traced path (migrated early-career, `trace --quantile 0.03`) shows the behaviour: 2052-2064 essential spending is $0 for 13 years while the household keeps paying $25k/yr of mortgage/tax/insurance through an overdraft that grows to $245k, with a $350-380k home throughout. What should happen: a household does not starve in a paid-for house; the headline success/depletion numbers and every buy-vs-rent comparison are biased against owning.
fix: Before cutting essentials in settle(), release home equity: if a Primary (then Vacation/Rental) property is owned, sell it through the existing PropertyModel::sell path (selling costs, exclusion, mortgage payoff), credit proceeds, and start a rent line (e.g. the owner's operating cost plus an imputed rent of ~4-5% of value, or a profile field `retirement.home_equity: never | last_resort | downsize_at_age`). Default it to last_resort. At minimum, report 'depleted with home equity > X' as a separate outcome and do not count it in the same bucket as true ruin, and show the equity in the failure explanation.

title: New York City residents are charged the 1.6% statewide average instead of the NYC tax: the city name from the app never matches the tax data
location: crates/firesight-core/src/tax/law.rs:1103-1115 (TaxLaw::local_rate matcher); data/tax/us-states-2026.json NY.local_income_tax.major_city = "New York City"; data/col/cities.csv:4004 city = "New York" (the list the web CitySearch uses); callers crates/firesight-core/src/sim/plan.rs:894 and :1130
evidence:
local_rate lower-cases and requires major == city or major.starts_with("<city> ("). Scratch output: law.local_rate(NY, Some("New York")) = 0.016, Some("NYC") = 0.016, Some("New York City") = 0.03876.
End to end: examples/early-career-saver.json with location NY / "New York" (/tmp/fs-audit-tax/nyc.json), `firesight trace nyc.json --path 0 --json`, 2027 return: 'local_income_tax 2,197 | 1.6% of state adjusted income 137,336'. Same profile with city "New York City": 5,322.
Hand calculation of the real NYC tax for that return: NYC taxable 137,336 - 8,000 = 129,336; 12,000 x 3.078% + 13,000 x 3.762% + 25,000 x 3.819% + 79,336 x 3.876% = 369 + 489 + 955 + 3,075 = 4,888. The engine under-taxes by $2,691 a year (55%). For a single filer on $400k the gap is 6,400 vs 15,069 = $8,669 a year.

Add a test that every major_city in us-states-2026.json resolves from the name used in data/col/cities.csv.

title: Local income tax is a flat rate on all state AGI: Portland is charged 4% from the first dollar, and wage-only city taxes are charged on retirement and investment income
location: crates/firesight-core/src/tax/calc.rs:445 (`o.local = st.local_rate * o.agi.max(0.0)`); data/tax/us-states-2026.json OR.local_income_tax.major_city_rate = 0.04 (also OH 0.025/0.012, PA 0.038712/0.0099, KY 0.0145/0.0093, MO 0.01, DE 0.0125, AL 0.01)
evidence:
Scratch (/tmp/fs-audit-tax/scratch/src/bin/t2.rs), params.state.local_rate = law.local_rate(state, city):
- Portland, joint wages 150k: local 6,000. Law: Metro SHS 1% and Multnomah PFA 1.5% apply only to taxable income above $200k joint / $125k single, so the true tax is 0. CLI: early-career-saver with OR/"Portland" (/tmp/fs-audit-tax/pdx.json), 2027: 'local_income_tax 5,490 | 4% of state adjusted income 137,245'; true tax about (137,245 - 2,910 - 125,000) x 2.5% = $233. Overstated by about $5,250 a year.
- Retired couple 67/67 with 50k IRA + 50k Social Security + 30k qualified dividends/long-term gains: Portland 3,200 (true 0); Columbus OH 2,000 (Ohio municipal tax reaches only wages and business profit: true 0); Kansas City 600 (earnings tax: true 0); Wilmington 688 (wage tax: true 0); Louisville 435 and Philadelphia 1,161 on the investment part (wage/occupational taxes; Philadelphia's school income tax would reach only the dividends).
In Ohio every resident gets the 1.2% statewide average, so a retiree with 80k of state AGI pays about $960 a year that does not exist. The module report states the simplification ('statewide average rate times state-adjusted income') but not these consequences.
fix: Add to the state data a `base` for the local tax (`earned` vs `all_income`) and optional thresholds. In state_tax compute local = rate x max(0, base - threshold) where the earned base is wages + self-employment profit. Mark OH, PA, KY, MO, DE, AL, MI as earned; MD, IN, NYC as all income; give Portland thresholds 125k/200k with 2.5% (and 4% above 250k/400k) on Oregon taxable income.

title: Roth conversions (and Illinois early distributions) are taxed by states that exempt retirement income
location: crates/firesight-core/src/tax/calc.rs:388 (`let retirement = x.traditional_distributions.max(0.0) + x.pensions.max(0.0);` leaves out roth_conversions); crates/firesight-core/src/tax/law.rs:707-710 (every taxed == "none" state gets the federal 59.5 age test)
evidence:
Scratch t2.rs, joint filers, 2026, 100,000 of income:
- IL age 62: conversion -> state tax 4,660.43; distribution -> 0.00. IL age 50: both 4,660.43.
- PA age 62: conversion 4,060.00 (3,070 state + 990 local); distribution 0.00.
- MS 2,936 vs 0; MI 3,908.50 vs 0; IA 2,576.40 vs 0. NY age 62: conversion 5,800.80 vs distribution 3,000.80 (the $20k-per-person exclusion is not applied to the conversion); CO 2,983 vs 1,223; GA 3,493 vs 0.
Law: Illinois subtracts amounts included in AGI from converting an IRA to a Roth IRA (35 ILCS 5/203(a)(2)(W), IDOR Publication 120) and has no age test for retirement-plan and IRA distributions, so all four Illinois figures should be 0. Pennsylvania does not tax a traditional-to-Roth conversion (PA Personal Income Tax Guide, REV-636).
The default withdrawal order is tax_aware with roth_conversions = true, so an Illinois household filling the 12% bracket with about 100k of conversions is charged about $4,700 a year of state tax that does not exist (about $4,100 in Pennsylvania), which also biases the conversion decision.
fix: Include roth_conversions in the income the state retirement exclusion applies to (calc.rs:388). Add a per-state flag for the age test instead of applying 59.5 to every exempt state: IL no age test; PA, MS 59.5; IA 55 (already in the data note). Add tests: IL conversion and IL early distribution give zero state tax; PA conversion at 62 gives zero.

title: Retirement plan budgets pre-65 health at full price, ignoring the ACA premium credit: households over-withdraw from retirement accounts and re-save the surplus in taxable, the HSA is drained tax-free, and guardrails cut discretionary to zero while the household is saving
location: crates/firesight-core/src/sim/year.rs:236-237 (run_rate health gross of credit), :631 (ess_annual), :672 (spend_month), :720 (net_need), :734 (medical_need = rate.health); credit only applied at payment time in crates/firesight-core/src/sim/month.rs:457-461; surplus swept in month.rs:1233-1245
evidence: spend_month and the spending rule's budget use rate.health (premium + out-of-pocket before the advance credit), but the household pays health_cost - advance. Dual-income path 3 (`firesight trace examples/dual-income-family.json --path 3`): 2051 planned health 57,127 vs spend_healthcare 12,684; withdrawals traditional 77,034 + Roth 38,141 + other 1,906 = 117,081 against spending 80,118 + tax 4,671 = 84,789; save_taxable 32,011. 2053: traditional 81,997 + Roth 37,407 withdrawn, spending 81,107, tax 4,960, save_taxable 33,820. Taxable balance grows 0 -> 194k between ages 56 and 65 while spend_discretionary is 0 in 2046-2055 (guardrail cut driven by the overstated budget). Across 1000 paths of the dual example, pre-65 retired years only: median $209,735 of traditional/Roth/HSA withdrawals re-saved to taxable in the same year (p25 141k, p75 259k; 96% of paths, median 10 years); 38% of paths have a year with discretionary at zero while re-saving. Early-career example: median $132,842; already-retired couple: $63,734 over 4 years (2027: Roth 20,078 withdrawn at 62, 15,405 saved to taxable). HSA: medical_need is the same gross figure, so HSA money is withdrawn as qualified far beyond what was paid: path 3 2047 withdraw_hsa 46,399 vs spend_healthcare 12,125; median lifetime excess $176,910 per path in the dual example (ACA premiums are not HSA-qualified in any case; before 65 the excess should be ordinary income plus 20% penalty). Sensitivity (private instrumented copy, credit of the previous year netted from rate.health, 3000 paths): constant_real success 88.0% -> 87.1% and median lifetime tax -$23k (the tax-free HSA leak currently flatters results); guardrails success 83.4% -> 74.4%, i.e. the flagship headline moves 9 points when this one input is corrected, because of the anchor defect above.
fix: In annual_plan compute the expected advance credit for the year before sizing the plan (iterate once: plan -> estimated MAGI -> credit -> re-plan, or use tax::compute on est_inputs as already done at year.rs:805 and loop) and subtract it from rate.health in ess_annual, spend_month, net_need and efund/cash-cap. Set medical_need to expected out-of-pocket only before 65 (premiums excluded; Medicare premiums allowed after 65), capped by actual health paid. Add a check-mode assertion that a retired household with no RMD does not both withdraw from tax-advantaged accounts and save to taxable above a tolerance in the same year.

title: Taxable windfall is withheld twice: 66% of a $5M windfall is taken in the month it arrives, and the $1.23M refund is booked as income the next April
location: crates/firesight-core/src/sim/events.rs:207-210 (adds windfall to ty.other_ordinary AND to wage_like), crates/firesight-core/src/sim/year.rs:788-796 (replan puts the whole remaining liability into wh_rate capped at 0.6 plus installment), crates/firesight-core/src/sim/month.rs:534 (prepay = wh_rate * wage_like + installment)
evidence: Repro: /tmp/fs-audit-ledger/p_s2_windfall.json (early-career example, events = one windfall of 5,000,000, taxable: true, 2028-06); `firesight trace p_s2_windfall.json --path 0 --json`. June 2028: income_other 5,000,000; tax_federal 2,936,781 + tax_state 357,795 = 3,294,576 (65.9%). The event triggers a replan whose estimate already contains the windfall, so the remaining tax becomes installment (rest/m_left) and wh_rate hits the 0.6 cap because wage_like_rest holds only the remaining salary; the month's wage_like then also contains the windfall, so 0.6 * 5.0M is withheld on top. Actual 2028 return: total 2,114,526 nominal. April 2029: income_other 1,230,650 (the refund). Effects: only 1,710,759 is invested instead of about 2.9M for ten months; investable_at_retirement is recorded as 1,674,101 (the funded test one month later sees wealth understated by $1.2M, which can delay FI on thinner plans); gross income double counts 1.23M; lifetime tax is overstated by the same amount.
fix: Do not add the windfall to wage_like (its tax is already in the replanned installment), or include it in wage_like_rest when computing wh_rate. Better: when an event adds taxable income, set aside exactly the marginal tax (tax::compute with and without it) in tax_reserve and pay it through the normal installments. Add a test that prepaid tax in the event month never exceeds the year's estimated liability.

title: Default Roth-conversion planner ignores capital-gain stacking: it converts at a true marginal cost of about 27%, and the default TaxAware order lowers success versus Conventional
location: crates/firesight-core/src/decumulation.rs:977-999 (conversion room = ordinary-bracket room only, tax sized at fill_rate), :1155-1189 (bracket_room from ordinary taxable income only); default set in crates/firesight-core/src/model/retirement.rs:241-249
evidence:
The conversion fills ordinary income to the top of the 12% bracket, which is also the top of the 0% long-term-gain bracket (2026 single: 50,400 vs 49,450). Every converted dollar therefore pushes a dollar of the gains realised by that year's taxable-account sales from 0% to 15%. The planner sizes the cost at fill_rate (12%) and never checks the real cost.

Unit repro (/tmp/fs-audit-decumulation/scratch/tests/conv.rs, real 2026 law, single, age 45, 600k taxable at 50% gain, 600k traditional, net need 60k):
- conversions off: from_taxable 60,000, tax 0, plus 35,550 of gains harvested free.
- conversions on: conversion 66,500, from_taxable 71,135, tax 11,135, harvest 0.
- Hand check: 66,500 - 16,100 deduction = 50,400 ordinary taxable -> 1,240 + 4,560 = 5,800; gains 35,568 x 15% = 5,335; total 11,135. That is 16.7% of the conversion (27% on the last 35.5k), against a later withdrawal rate of roughly 8-12% for this household, and the free 0% harvest is lost.

Full simulation (/tmp/fs-audit-decumulation/p/base.json: single, 40, TX, 150k salary, 400k taxable with 250k basis, 500k traditional, 100k Roth, 60k budget, healthcare in budget, default when_funded 4%; `firesight compare base.json conv.json noconv.json --paths 5000`):
- TaxAware default: success 90.7%. Conventional: 91.6% (44 rescued, 0 harmed). TaxAware with roth_conversions=false: 91.6% (47 rescued, 0 harmed). So the whole loss comes from conversions.
- Median terminal net worth 2.905M vs 3.213M; p25 0.995M vs 1.171M; Conventional ends richer in 68% of paired paths. Caveat: terminal net worth counts traditional balances pre-tax, so this gap overstates the after-tax difference; the success-rate loss is the clean evidence.
- Median lifetime tax is lower with conversions (249k vs 380k), but TaxAware pays more lifetime tax in 34% of paths, and those are the poor paths.
- Path 307: federal tax in the first eight retirement years is 9.1k-15.7k a year with conversions against 0-3.7k under Conventional. Its 2029 return shows 13,750 at 10% + 42,200 at 12% + 9,288 at 22%, plus 70,570 of gains all at 15% (10,586). The path depletes at 66.9 under TaxAware and survives under Conventional.
- fill_to_bracket 0.22 is worse again: success -1.8 points, median terminal net worth -323k.

The funded test (trigger.rs:262-303) budgets only the tax on spending withdrawals and does not include this conversion tax, so the household retires on a requirement that excludes it.

The lever behaves as theory predicts where the stacking is absent: with no embedded gains (bigtrad.json: 55, 2M traditional, 800k taxable at full basis) conversions cut median lifetime tax 1.056M -> 0.884M and raise median terminal net worth by 95k. With ACA modelled (aca.json) the cliff caps conversions and they help success by 0.8 points. On the shipped examples: early-career-saver loses 0.8 points of success to conversions, dual-income-family gains 3.5.
fix: Size the conversion on its real marginal cost. Cap conversion room at min(ordinary-bracket room, 0%-gain room = capital_gains zero_top - taxable income including the year's planned gains and qualified dividends) whenever the plan realises preferential income. Or, as the harvest step already does at decumulation.rs:1250-1258, evaluate tax::compute with and without the conversion and keep only the part whose incremental tax (plus lost ACA credit) per converted dollar is at or below fill_rate plus a small tolerance. Add the expected conversion tax to the funded test, or leave conversions out until the test accounts for them. Add a common-random-number regression test that TaxAware does not have lower success than Conventional on a household with appreciated taxable assets.

title: Guardrails, Vanguard-dynamic and floor-ceiling take their reference withdrawal rate from the first retirement year, so a partner who keeps working makes them cut spending permanently
location: crates/firesight-core/src/decumulation.rs:290-301 (start), :351-354 (IWR set once), :365-381 (guardrails), :391-401 (Vanguard), :417-425 (floor-ceiling); caller crates/firesight-core/src/sim/year.rs:633-650 (other_income includes the partner's wages)
evidence:
initial_withdrawal_rate = (budget - other income) / portfolio in the first retired year and is never re-based. With partner_offset_years > 0 (or any temporary income at retirement), other income nearly covers the budget, so the reference rate is close to zero. When that income stops, the true withdrawal rate is far above 1.2 x the reference and the capital-preservation rule cuts 10% every year down to essentials. The same happens with the Vanguard floor (-2.5% a year) and floor-ceiling (pinned at its 85% floor).

Unit repro (/tmp/fs-audit-decumulation/scratch/tests/unit.rs, guardrails_partner_bridge): budget 80k, partner nets 76k for 3 years, portfolio 2M earning 4% real, so a 4% rate is exactly sustainable. Reference rate = 0.002. Guardrails spending: 80,000 for 3 years, then 72,000, 64,800, 58,320 ... 30,994 by year 11 while the portfolio grows from 2.24M to 2.56M. Vanguard falls 2.5% a year to 63,945. Floor-ceiling sits at 68,000 for good.

Full simulation (/tmp/fs-audit-decumulation/p/c2_*.json: couple aged 50, about 2M, 80k budget of which 48k essential, person 0 retires now, partner earns 95k for 4 more years; `firesight run --paths 3000`), spending delivered as a share of plan:
- Guardrails: 68.2% with the 4-year offset against 157.7% with no offset; 99.9% of paths have a year below 90%.
- Vanguard dynamic: 84.4% against 173.6%.
- Floor-ceiling: 90.5% against 113.1%.
- Constant real: 100% in both.
Trace of path 3 (c2_gk_4.json): discretionary spending goes 28.5k -> 18.3k -> 11.7k -> 5.7k -> 0.3k -> 0 and stays at zero from age 59 with investable of 4.6M-10M and 89k of Social Security. The household that works longer ends up with far lower spending than the one that does not, which is the wrong sign.

Guyton-Klinger itself is correct against the published rules when there is no other income (see verified list).
fix: Define the reference rate on the steady state, not on the first retired year. Either exclude income that is known to end (wages of a still-working partner, jobs with ends_at_retirement=false, bridge income) when computing initial_withdrawal_rate in start() and at :351, or re-base it (initial_withdrawal_rate = planned_withdrawal / portfolio) in the January after earned income stops, and floor it at a sane minimum such as the trigger's withdrawal rate. Add a sim test that with partner_offset_years > 0 delivered spending is not lower than with offset 0.

title: 72(t): a fresh penalty-free tranche is granted every year on top of the running schedule, so early-withdrawal penalties nearly vanish after year one

This breaks the documented contract 'run_path is a pure function of its arguments' and 'run_range a..b + b..c == a..c'.

Measured on a realistic retired couple (dual-income example with births 1961-09/1962-04, no jobs/children/events, $2.43M across the same accounts, known_benefit SS $2,600, trigger already_retired; file /tmp/fs-audit-perf-determinism/fz/retired.json, validates with 0 errors): every path starts from the identical balance sheet so the 'funded ratio at retirement' must be one number. With the fix below: 1.5636 on all 2,000 paths, reused or fresh workspace. So the reported funded ratio is off by -11.6%..+4.1% per path, and a household whose true ratio is near 1.0 gets its 'financially independent' flag (fi_month at t=0, trigger.rs / month.rs:675) set or not depending on the neighbouring path.

Thread-count variance in the CLI (the determinism requirement): `firesight run retired.json --paths 10000 --threads {1,4,10} --summary-out` gives three different Summary files (sha1 c7369499ab / 9cb8754261 / e5a547a872). Repro: `cd /tmp/fs-audit-perf-determinism && target-h/release/fr fz/retired.json` (prints the per-path ratios), `target-h/release/inv fz/t.jsonl`, or the CLI commands above.

title: Survivor benefits are understated in three ways (double reduction with the widow's limit, permanent age-60 reduction for a widow whose benefits were all withheld, 35-year averaging for a worker who dies young)
location: crates/firesight-core/src/benefits.rs:1045-1071 (survivor branch of `monthly`), :282-295 (`EarningsRecord::aime`)
evidence:
All three reproduced with scratch binaries against `SocialSecurityModel::monthly` (/tmp/fs-audit-people/scratch/src/bin/ss2.rs, ss4.rs, ss5.rs). Each errs on the conservative side and only matters on paths where one spouse dies early.

(a) Widow's limit applied multiplicatively.
- Case: deceased PIA 3,000, claimed at 62 (70%); widow aged 63 at the death; survivor full retirement age 67.
- Engine: base = max(2,100, 82.5% x 3,000) = 2,475, then x age factor 0.8371 = 2,071.93 a month.
- SSA rule (POMS RS 00615.320): benefit = min(PIA x age factor, widow's limit) = min(2,511.43, 2,475) = 2,475.
- Engine is 16.3% low.

(b) Survivor benefit forced to start at 60 and the reduction never undone.
- Case: deceased PIA 3,000, died unclaimed at 57; widow the same age, earning 100k until 67.
- Engine: withholds 2,145 a month for all 84 months from 60 to 67 (paid 0, withheld 180,180), then pays 2,145 (71.5%) for life.
- SSA: she would either not file until 67 or have the reduction removed at full retirement age for every withheld month, so 3,000.
- Engine is 28.5% low for life. The 84 withheld months are also added to `Claimant::withheld_months`, which is meant to adjust her own retirement claim.

(c) Death before 62 uses 35 computation years.
- Case: born 1981, earned exactly the average wage 2003-2025, dies in 2026.
- Engine: AIME = 23 years / 420 months = 3,987 (2025 wage dollars).
- SSA: computation years = elapsed years (23) minus 5 = 18, so AIME = 6,067. On the 2026 formula that is a PIA of 2,608 against 1,970 on the engine's basis.
- The survivor's base is 24.5% low.
fix:
(a) Compute `survivor = min(partner_pia * age_factor, max(partner_actual_benefit, widow_floor * partner_pia))` when the deceased had claimed early, and `base * factor` otherwise.
(b) Do not start the survivor benefit while the earnings test would withhold all of it (start at the later of 60, the death, and the survivor's retirement), or recompute the age factor at survivor full retirement age net of withheld months. Keep survivor withholding out of `withheld_months` for the own claim.
(c) When the worker dies before 62, divide by max(2, elapsed years - 5) x 12 months and index to the year two years before death.

Plausibility of the history: the engine credits a 37-year-old on 150k with 66,579 nominal in 2012 at age 22, which is 1.50 times that year's average wage (about 95k in today's dollars). The steep profile gives 40,300 (0.91 times).

Two related gaps in the same lines:
- `WageGrowth::Flat { real_raise }` is backfilled as constant real pay, ignoring `real_raise`. A 60-year-old on 150k flat is then at the taxable maximum for most of 1989-2010 and gets a PIA of 4,328, above the 4,217 of a maximum earner born in 1964.
- `Lifecycle.extra` is ignored.

The error shrinks as simulated years replace rebuilt ones. It matters most for early-retirement paths and for the funded test, which counts the present value of the benefit.
fix: In `Plan::compile`, build the record with `EarningsRecord::backfill_with(earnings, age, career_start_age, &ss, |a| career_curve(a))`, using the same `JobModel` curve the simulation uses going forward, including `extra` and a flat `real_raise`. Delete the separate profile table in benefits.rs. Add a test that the last rebuilt year and the first simulated year lie on one curve.

title: A household with no earned income at the start gets the lowest USDA child-cost tier whatever it spends
location: crates/firesight-core/src/sim/plan.rs:746-752 (tier chosen from `income_rate0`, the sum of job and self-employment pay at start)
evidence:
Repro: /tmp/fs-audit-people/retired45kids.json. Already-retired couple aged 45, 3.5M in assets, a 108,000 a year budget, two children aged 8 and 10 with `costs: modeled`. Run `./target/release/firesight trace /tmp/fs-audit-people/retired45kids.json --path 1 --json`.

- Engine: `spend_children` is 15,863 in 2027, about 7.3-8.2k per child. That is the low-income tier (5,250 and 5,880 in 2015 dollars, times about 1.39).
- High tier for the same ages: 9,910 and 11,230 in 2015 dollars, about 29,700 a year for the two.
- Understatement: about 13,800 a year until the children are 18, roughly 130k for this family.

The same happens to anyone between jobs at the start month, and the tier never changes afterwards. Households with jobs at the start are tiered correctly: the dual-income example, on 229k, gets the high tier and its 2027 child cost of 33,253 matches the hand calculation (9,160 x 1.39 x 1.27 only-child factor + 16,800 childcare).
fix: Choose the tier from the larger of earned income and the household's planned annual spending grossed up to pre-tax income (or simply from total budget against USDA's expenditure-based boundaries). At minimum, use the high tier when retired with investable assets above about 25 times the middle-tier income.

title: Paths are cut at the youngest adult's 100th birthday: 14-20% of couples are still alive, their death age is reported as 100, and end-of-life care scheduled after 100 is never charged
location: crates/firesight-core/src/sim/plan.rs:500-501 (`horizon_months` from `simulation.end_age`, default 100); crates/firesight-core/src/sim/state.rs:487 (`self.months = last.min(plan.horizon_months)`); crates/firesight-core/src/health.rs:1078-1087 (episode scheduled back from the uncapped death month)
evidence:
Repro: `./target/release/firesight run /tmp/fs-audit-people/retired.json --paths 20000 --json` (couple aged 65.8, default good health, improvement on).

- `survival.household` in the last year is 0.182: on 18% of paths someone is still alive when the run stops.
- The `death_age_0` and `death_age_1` distributions have `max` 100 and their top quantiles are all exactly 100.
- From the survival curves: P(at least one of a couple alive at 100) is 14.3% for a couple aged 65 and 19.8% for a couple aged 35 with default settings.

The care episode is placed in the last months before the true death. For anyone who dies after 100, part or all of it lies beyond the horizon and is not charged. These are the people with the highest care probability (0.67 or more for deaths at 85+).

Measured effect: mean lifetime care cost for this couple is 312k in the simulation, against 340k from 200,000 uncapped lives per sex with the same model (about 8% lower; a small part of the gap is the 65.8 against 65.0 start age). The truncated paths also skip about 2.5-3 years of spending and are counted as successes.
fix: Run each path to the last death (the life table already ends at 120), or default `end_age` to the table's end and keep it only as an advanced cap. If a cap stays, report death ages above it as censored rather than as the cap, and charge the part of a care episode that falls inside the horizon by scheduling it back from min(death, horizon) when death is beyond the horizon.

title: The 1.5% a year age gradient after 65 is applied to Part B and Part D premiums, which do not vary with age
location: crates/firesight-core/src/health.rs:776-788 (`medicare_age_factor`), :974-978 and :1133 (premium x scale)
evidence:
`price()` returns one `scale` = 1.015^(age-65) for the whole Medicare phase and `step()` multiplies both premium and out-of-pocket by it. Of the 7,318 a year at 65, 2,935 is the Part B premium (202.90 x 12 = 2,435) plus Part D (500). CMS sets these per beneficiary regardless of age; only Medigap (attained-age rating) and out-of-pocket use rise with age.

Engine output (`expected_annual_cost`, today's dollars, no excess inflation): 7,318 at 65, 8,493 at 75, 9,856 at 85, 10,618 at 90.

Hand calculation of the overstatement:
- At 90: 2,935 x (1.015^25 - 1) = 1,324 a year, 12.5% of the 10,618.
- Over 21 years from 65, with 1.5% excess inflation on everything: 2,935 x (sum of 1.030225^k minus sum of 1.015^k, k = 0..20) = 2,935 x (28.75 - 23.47) = 15,500 of 210,400, or 7.4%.
- Over 30 years (to 95): about 30,000 of 349,000, or 8.6%.
- For someone aged 35 today these amounts are 1.56 times larger in today's dollars.

This is a calibration choice in the data ("real cost rises about 1.5%/yr with age", marked judgement), and the total at 65 still agrees with Fidelity. The bias grows with age and so falls on the long-lived paths that decide depletion risk.
fix: Apply the age factor to the Medigap premium and the out-of-pocket mean only. Keep Part B and D at 1.0 by age (they still get excess medical inflation). If the 21-year total is meant to stay near 210k, raise the gradient on the age-rated part to about 2.5% and document it.

title: Children carry no health insurance cost, which understates an unsubsidised early retiree's bill by about 5,000 per child per year
location: crates/firesight-core/src/health.rs:33-34 and :967-973 (adults only); crates/firesight-core/src/sim/month.rs:400-440 (loop over adults); crates/firesight-core/src/sim/year.rs:279 (children counted in the ACA household size but not in the benchmark)
evidence:
Repro: /tmp/fs-audit-people/retired45kids.json, trace path 1. In 2032 the couple (both 50) is above the 400% cliff and `spend_healthcare` is 28,438. That equals two adults only: 2 x (982 x 12 + 1,200) x 1.015^5.5 = 28,200.

The CMS age curve in the data prices a child aged 0-14 at 0.765 / 1.278 x 703 = 421 a month, or 5,050 a year (the data's own `derived_unsubsidised_benchmark_annual_2027.child_0_14` is 5,057). Two children add about 11,000 a year in 2032 dollars, 39% more than the engine charges. They would also raise the benchmark used for the credit.

For subsidised households the error is small: the family pays the income-based contribution either way, and the children are already in the household size at year.rs:279. The gap is for households above the cliff. The same omission applies while working: each adult pays the single-coverage worker share (2 x 1,765 = 3,530) against KFF's family contribution of 7,471.

The module documents this as a simplification, on the grounds that USDA child costs include health care. The core cost does carry USDA's health line (1,440-1,820 per child in 2015 dollars for the high tier), which is out-of-pocket and employer-plan cost-sharing, not a marketplace premium.
fix: In the ACA phase add `aca_benchmark_monthly(child_age) x tier factor` for up to three children under 21 (CMS rule) to both the premium and `aca_benchmark_premium`. In the employer phase use the family worker contribution when the household has children or a non-working partner.

title: Taxable items of an event dated in January land on the previous year's tax return
location: crates/firesight-core/src/sim/month.rs:103-111 (run_events executes before annual_plan, which closes the prior tax year in January via sim/year.rs:373); items affected: sim/events.rs:146-152 (sale gain, recapture, released passive losses) and :204-210 (taxable windfall)
evidence: Repro /tmp/fs-audit-work-home/t1.json: single owner, primary home value 800,000, basis 300,000, sell_property dated 2030-01, 6% costs. `firesight trace t1.json --path 0 --json`: event log shows 'sold_home' in 2030-01, but tax_returns[year=2029] carries 'Capital gains 329,783' (and NIIT 9,508, IRMAA tier 4) while the 2030 return has long-term gains of 372. The gain is stacked on the wrong year's income and the tax is settled a year early (April 2030 instead of April 2031). The amounts themselves are right (see verified list).
fix: In State::month, when month == 1 && t > 0, close the previous tax year (the close_tax_year / roll_year part of annual_plan) before run_events, then run events, then do the forward-looking part of the annual plan; or have fire() write into a 'next year' TaxInputs when called before the January close.

title: v1 migration: budget lines silently grow faster than inflation, contradicting the migration notes (the 'Mortgage (PITI)' line, healthcare and childcare)
location: crates/firesight-core/src/legacy.rs:686 ('rent' | 'mortgage' => Category::Rent), :694 (name contains 'child' => Childcare), :715-717 (note text), items pushed with real_growth None so crates/firesight-core/src/model/spending.rs:329-336 applies +0.5% (rent), +1.5% (healthcare), +1.0% (childcare) real per year
evidence: `firesight migrate examples/v1/dual-income-family.json`: the note says the PITI line 'is imported as a housing cost that rises with inflation and never ends', and v1's expenditure_growth_beyond_inflation was 0.0, but the migrated items have real_growth null. Trace (path 5) essential spending in today's dollars: 2032 $82,689 -> 2044 $88,522 -> 2056 $96,138 (+16%). title: Lifecycle wage curves peak at 45 and fall 15% (Typical) to 22% (Steep) in real terms by 65; the schema describes them as 'slightly declining after the mid-50s'
location: crates/firesight-core/src/model/income.rs (WageGrowth::Lifecycle and LifecycleProfile doc comments); crates/firesight-core/src/career.rs:340-353, 366-371
evidence: career::lifecycle_factor on the embedded coefficients (scratch/src/bin/career.rs): Typical 25->55 x1.663, 30->40 x1.308, 40->50 x1.005, 45->55 x0.934, 55->65 x0.911, 45->65 x0.851, peak age 45. Steep: 25->55 x2.031, 45->55 x0.911, 55->65 x0.854, 45->65 x0.778, peak 45. A 45-year-old on the default profile therefore loses 0.8%/yr of real pay until 65 (1.2%/yr on Steep) before any shocks or layoffs; on top of that the measured mean of simulated base pay is 10% below the curve after 20 years at Typical risk. The numbers match CGM (household labour income, including reduced hours near retirement) and Guvenen et al. for median earners, so this is a description/default issue, not an arithmetic one, but the text understates it and 'Steep' (described as professional careers) declines fastest, whereas Guvenen's high lifetime earners keep growing to 55.
fix: Correct the schema text (peak in the mid-40s; about -1%/yr real afterwards). Consider holding Steep flat after its peak (CGM's late decline largely reflects hours and retirement, which the simulation models separately through the retirement date), and show the implied pay at 55/65 in the preview so users over 45 can override with Flat or `extra`.

title: Throughput: dual-income is at ~5,200 paths/s per core native and ~3,150 in wasm; 8,000 is not reachable with fidelity-preserving micro-optimisation (best measured 6,018 with four prototypes + PGO)
location: crates/firesight-core/src/sim/year.rs:333-865 (annual_plan, 32.5% of run time), crates/firesight-core/src/decumulation.rs:1095-1250 (plan_year, 12.2%), crates/firesight-core/src/tax/law.rs:936-1035 (for_year, 6.5%), crates/firesight-core/src/accounts.rs:744-795 (apply_returns, ~11% incl. the stall it causes), workspace Cargo.toml [profile.release]
evidence:
Apple M4, single thread, best of 7 x 3,000 paths, scratch harness /tmp/fs-audit-perf-determinism/h/src/bin/bench.rs (other reviewers were loading the machine: load average 5-35, so treat +-1% as noise; the repo's own `firesight bench` printed 4,421 / 4,669 / 6,137 paths/s under that load). Baseline dual-income 5,182 paths/s (193 us/path, 284 ns per month-step), early-career 5,721, side-hustle 6,185. wasm (node 25, wasm-pack release, wasm-opt -O3): 3,150 / 3,105 / 4,428 = 0.55-0.72x native.

The profile is flat (see measurements): no single hot spot above 12%. Per dual-income path there are 60.5 annual_plan calls, 41.3 plan_year calls, 80.2 gross-up evaluations and 369.5 tax returns computed (~73 ns each).

Prototypes in a scratch copy (diff: /tmp/fs-audit-perf-determinism/prototype.diff, 281 lines; all keep the accumulator bytes identical to the repo code on all three examples at 20,000 paths, pass the crate's full test suite (366 unit + integration tests) and 1,964 fuzz profiles x 30 paths with the conservation check on):
1. TaxLaw::for_year_into(&mut TaxYearParams) writing in place instead of building a 3,752-byte value and copying it twice: 5,173 -> 5,307 (+2.6%).
2. plan_year: generic tax function instead of `&dyn Fn`, and the gross-up evaluation written into one reusable struct instead of returning a 1.5 KB tuple: 5,307 -> 5,305 (no measurable gain).
3. Pass the base TaxResult annual_plan has already computed (year.rs:611) into plan_year instead of recomputing the identical return (decumulation.rs:1103): 5,297 -> 5,362 (+1.2%).
4. apply_returns: `inc.net_change` and `inc.fees` are one serial chain of 63 floating-point adds (7 buckets x 9 asset classes, ~190 cycles of latency that stalls the out-of-order window; the wait shows up as 6.5% in apply_returns plus 4.7% in track_portfolio). Summing per asset class first (nine chains of 7, then 9 adds): 5,364 -> 5,558 (+3.6%). This reorders a sum, so it is not bit-identical in principle; balances are untouched and the accumulator bytes were identical on all three examples at 20k paths.
Cumulative 1-4: 5,182 -> 5,552 (+7.1%); early-career 5,721 -> 6,188 (+8.2%); side-hustle 6,185 -> 6,681 (+8.0%).
5. PGO (-Cprofile-generate, 1,500 paths of each example, Homebrew llvm-profdata 23.1.5 matching rustc's LLVM, -Cprofile-use) on top: 6,018 / 6,550 / 7,465 (+16.1% / +14.5% / +20.7% over baseline, same accumulator hashes). PGO alone on the baseline code: +5.2%.
No gain: -Ctarget-cpu=native (5,528 vs 5,541); wasm +simd128,+bulk-memory,+nontrapping-fptoint (3,150 -> 3,166, bytes identical); wasm-opt -O3 vs --no-opt (+1%). Prototypes 1-2 in wasm: 3,054 -> 3,212 (+5%).

So 5,000/core is met natively by a thin margin and not met in the browser; 8,000 on dual-income needs structural change, not flags.
fix: Take prototypes 1, 3 and 4 as they are (+7%), and ship the native CLI with PGO (+8% more) if the build can carry the extra step. Beyond that, the next candidates in order of the measured profile, none prototyped (estimates are upper bounds from the profile shares, not measurements): (a) plan_year is 12.2% of run time at ~2 gross-up evaluations per year, each a full allocate + execute_plan on an 800-byte Accounts copy + a tax return; reuse the forced/bracket-room returns between evaluations and skip the 0%-gain-harvest probe when result.taxable_income is already above the 0% top: up to ~4%. (b) for_year still indexes all filing statuses and both bracket tables every January (4% left after prototype 1); index only the status in force and re-index on a status change: ~2-3%. (c) Accounts::contribute re-normalises the same target mix (9 divides) on every call, 3.8% of time; cache the normalised target once per plan year: ~2%. (d) Accounts::by_kind / investable is computed up to three times per month (month.rs:580, trigger, record): ~2%. (e) the remaining 5.5% memmove is mostly TaxInputs/PlanInputs/WithdrawalPlan copies in annual_plan (year.rs:545, 707-741). For wasm specifically, simd and wasm-opt settings are exhausted; the gap to native is V8 code quality on branchy scalar code, so the same source-level changes are the lever (wasm-pack strips the name section even with --profiling, so I could not attribute wasm time per function).

title: validate() panics instead of reporting out_of_range when a `When` age/offset is astronomically large (overflow-checked builds only)
location: crates/firesight-core/src/model/time.rs:65 (YearMonth::add_years_f64: `self.0 + (years * 12.0).round() as i32`), reached from validate.rs:249 (Checker::window -> When::resolve -> at_age, time.rs:85/268)
evidence: Found by the fuzzer (4 hits in ~17,000 candidates). Minimal repro: dual-income example with spending.items[0].start = {"type":"age","person":0,"age":1e9} and end = {"type":"age","person":0,"age":2e9} (/tmp/fs-audit-perf-determinism/fz/min_overflow.jsonl). In a build with overflow checks (dev/test profile, or my fuzz harness built with overflow-checks=true): `panicked at model/time.rs:65:14: attempt to add with overflow` inside validate(), because the f64->i32 cast saturates to i32::MAX and the add overflows. In the release build and the shipped wasm the add wraps and validate returns the correct `out_of_range` error for the age (confirmed through wasm applyPatch for ages 150 .. 1e308 and -1e9), so production users are not affected; a dev-profile wasm or `cargo test` on such input aborts.
fix: Use saturating arithmetic in add_years_f64 and add_months (`self.0.saturating_add(...)`), or skip the window-order check in Checker::window when either bound already failed its range check. Add a unit test validating a profile with age 1e308 under the test profile.
